messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tariq still remembers the night the call came in. He was five years on the job, a paramedic in a busy city, and he and his partner were dispatched to a multi-car collision on the interstate. What he hadn't known until he arrived was that his younger brother, Amir, had been driving home from a late shift. Tariq found him pinned in the wreckage, conscious, bleeding from a deep gash across his scalp, his leg twisted under the dashboard. Tariq worked the scene, his hands moving on autopilot, but what he saw—the open wound, the way his brother's eyes looked through him, the smell of gasoline mixing with the antiseptic from the trauma kit—etched itself into him. He remembers the terror of that moment, the same cold terror that now floods back whenever the memory surfaces, and it feels completely real across all his senses at once. There are parts of that night he cannot piece together no matter how hard he tries—the exact sequence of extrication, who cut the roof off the car—but the image of Amir's face, the smell of the hospital corridor afterward, those are seared into him.

In the months that followed, Tariq returned to work, but the job itself became a minefield. Every visible injury on a patient—a laceration, a compound fracture—sends him straight back to that night. He catches the antiseptic smell of the hospital on his uniform and his stomach tightens, his concentration scattering like leaves in wind. He has come to believe that he has permanently changed for the worse, that something essential in him broke that night and cannot be fixed. He is certain he cannot rely on himself anymore, because if he could not protect his own brother, what good is he? The thought that he failed to protect Amir—that he should have done more, should have gotten him out faster—is a weight he carries constantly. These appraisals make the triggers worse: every time he sees a victim's face, he thinks of Amir's face, and the cycle tightens.

When a patient comes in with visible wounds, Tariq's body reacts before his mind can catch up. He flinches if a colleague touches his shoulder unexpectedly, and he finds himself scanning the ambulance bay for a seat with his back to the wall, a position where no one can approach from behind. This hypervigilance feeds the memory: the more on edge he feels, the more vividly the sensory reliving returns. He can smell the antiseptic, hear his brother's labored breathing, feel the weight of the trauma shears in his hand. The memory then reinforces his negative appraisals—he remembers his hands shaking, remembers the delay, and tells himself again that he failed.

To cope, Tariq has developed strategies that only deepen the problem. He throws himself into work, taking extra shifts, volunteering for the busiest runs, keeping his mind occupied so he doesn't have to think. But overworking means he is constantly exposed to triggers, and the suppressed thoughts only push the memory down until it bursts back stronger. He tries hard not to think about the trauma, but the effort of suppression exhausts him, and the memories intrude anyway, often at night when he is alone. He has started avoiding going to work when he can, calling in sick, trading shifts with colleagues. This avoidance gives him temporary relief, but it also confirms to him that he cannot handle the job, that he is broken, that he failed. The more he avoids, the more he believes he cannot rely on himself, and the more he scans for threats when he does return.

His wife has noticed the change. She tells him he seems distant, that he flinches when she touches him in bed. He has stopped talking about his brother. At work, his supervisor has pulled him aside twice about missed shifts. What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a moment last week: he was driving home after a shift and saw a car with a dented fender on the side of the road, and for a split second he was sure it was Amir's car, and the terror hit him so hard he had to pull over. He sat in his own vehicle, shaking, the smell of antiseptic phantom in his nose, and he realized he cannot keep living this way. He is afraid that if he does not get help, he will lose his job, his marriage, and any sense of himself that remains. But what frightens him most is the thought that talking about it will make it real all over again, and he is not sure he can survive that.
